chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: The baritone saxophone in the section; how Duke wrote for it
summary: He traces baritone doubling with Henderson, Teddy Hill and Kirby, praises how Ellington wrote for baritone and his mixed voicings, and mentions Satin Doll.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: But Benny -- but Benny -- of course he played saxophone, then he had three in the section, so:that made four saxophones, which was a tenor and three altos. Then later on, I think Duke Ellington was the first, one of the first -- I can't actually say that he was the first -- to add a baritone to the saxophone section. Of course Fletcher, we had baritones, Hilton Jefferson and I had baritones when we worked with Fletcher, but they were just doubles. We weren't baritone players as such all the time, and the arrangements weren't written for baritones all the way through. They were just double. In fact we just played them sometimes, doubled on them. And when I was with Teddy Hill's band I took the baritone and doubled on it.
But then when I joined Kirby's band I had the baritone there too for awhile, but I just played choruses, solos on it, you know, because the music was written for the alto.
And it was fun, you know, playing it.

Well, incidentally, talking about the baritone, I used to like sometimes when Harry Carney was away from Duke's band, I used to love to play the baritone, because I never saw anyone write for baritone like Duke used to write. Oh, he was beautiful. He wrote for the baritone like it was a saxophone, which it is. And these other people who wrote for baritone, they would be -- they would write for it like it was a bass. You know, you'd play the bass line. But Duke wrote for it as a -- so Benny had four saxophones, which is four-part harmony, then later on the five-part harmony came. Then all the bands had baritone, two tenors and two altos, so I guess they figured from that, because it was the best voicing or the best sound, or whatever. Well, it didn't matter, actually, what the saxophones were, because I figure that if an arranger wanted to get a sound, a certain sound, he could get it out of more than one array of saxophones, like Duke used to write, write, write, he wrote a whole lot of music, and he also added baritone, two tenors and two altos. But you never could tell, really, who was playing the lead. He wrote -- Duke wrote a whole lot of things. He'd have, like I say, the baritone, two tenors and two altos, and it might be a tenor playing the lead with the same array of saxophones. The baritone would have the lead doubling with a tenor playing the lead. Then the two altos and one tenor would be playing the harmony. A different
mixture. That's what Duke used to call it, a mixture, a mixture.

Like I remember distinctly, "Satin Doll," when he came up with the arrangement on, "Satin Doll," that was one of them. The tenor saxophone played the lead. And listening to it you wouldn't realize that. You know, unless it was a musician who just analyzed it and came up with that thing. Yeah. Yeah.

So then it became very popular to have a baritone saxophone player, a full time baritone, let's put it that way, a full time baritone saxophone player. Then all the bands, the baritone and two saxophones, two tenors and two altos became standard, and that was it. Yeah.
